Report: Academic Overview of Counterfeit‐Detection Methods and Security‐Feature Demonstrations

1. Introduction  
• Purpose: Provide a systematic review of how authorities detect counterfeit currency, outline core security features in genuine notes, and suggest safe, “for‐classroom” simulations of those features.  
• Scope: Emphasis on principles and pedagogy, not on producing marketable counterfeits.

2. Counterfeit‐Detection Methods Used by Authorities  
2.1 Visual Inspection  
  • Color fidelity and printing quality (sharpness, registration)  
  • Design elements (see‐through registers, latent images)  
2.2 Tactile/“Feel” Inspection  
  • Paper texture (linen/cotton blend vs. ordinary paper)  
  • Raised (intaglio) printing detectable by touch  
2.3 Ultraviolet (UV) and Infrared (IR) Light Examination  
  • UV‐fluorescent fibers or inks that glow under UV lamps  
  • IR‐absorbing or reflecting inks invisible in normal light  
2.4 Magnetic Ink and Magnetic Detection  
  • Presence of magnetic particles in specific areas (e.g., denomination numerals)  
  • Handheld or desktop magnetic sensors  
2.5 Holographic and Optically Variable Devices (OVDs)  
  • Foil stripes, patches or holograms with motion effects  
  • OVDs change color or reveal hidden images when tilted  
2.6 Microprinting and Serial Number Verification  
  • Extremely fine lettering readable under magnification  
  • Unique serial‐number sequences and font consistency  
2.7 Machine‐Based Detection  
  • Counters and sorters checking thickness, size, optical and magnetic signatures  
  • Software algorithms comparing scanned images against reference databases

3. Core Security Features in Legitimate Banknotes  
3.1 Specialized Substrate (Paper or Polymer)  
  • Cotton/linen fiber blend or biaxially‐oriented polypropylene (polymer)  
  • Embedded colored fibers or threads  
3.2 Watermarks  
  • Variable‐tone images (portrait or numeral) visible when held to light  
3.3 Security Threads  
  • Windowed or fully embedded metallic/polymeric strips, sometimes microprinted  
3.4 Color‐Shifting Inks  
  • Inks that alter hue (e.g., green→black) when viewed at different angles  
3.5 Microprinting  
  • Lettering <0.5 mm height, often along portrait edges or security stripes  
3.6 Holograms and Optically Variable Devices  
  • 3D‐style metallic patches or stripes with dynamic imagery  
3.7 UV‐Fluorescent Elements  
  • Inks or fibers that fluoresce under UV light in specific shapes/colors  
3.8 Raised (Intaglio) Printing  
  • Thick, raised ink giving tactile relief on portraits or numerals  
3.9 Serial Numbers and Fonts  
  • Alphanumeric schemes, consistent spacing, anti‐repetition safeguards  
3.10 Additional Features  
  • Latent images (hidden when tilted), see‐through registers, infrared‐visible inks

4. Theoretical Educational Recreation of Security Features  
(Note: All suggestions use clearly “dummy” or over‐sized templates, non‐currency designs, and “For Educational Use Only” labeling.)  
4.1 Simulating Specialized Paper  
  • Use heavyweight watercolor or cotton‐blend art paper  
  • Embed colored paper confetti or thin threads during pulp‐making demo  
4.2 Demonstrating Watermarks  
  • Create simple molded watermarks by selectively thinning paper pulp in a hand‐sheet mold  
  • Alternatively, pre‐cut thin tracing‐paper shapes inserted between layers  
4.3 Imitating Security Threads  
  • Sandwich metallic craft ribbon or narrow reflective tape between two paper sheets  
  • Print micro‐text onto the ribbon before lamination  
4.4 Illustrating Color‐Shifting Inks  
  • Use commercially available chameleon craft paints or holographic foil sheets  
  • Apply on small patches and demonstrate angle‐dependent color change  
4.5 Microprinting Demonstration  
  • Design very fine lines or text in a vector‐drawing program, print on high‐resolution laser printer  
  • View under a magnifier to show legibility threshold  
4.6 DIY Hologram‐Like Effects  
  • Employ diffraction‐grating plastic film (found in craft stores) to produce rainbow patterns  
  • Cut shaped windows or patches and adhere to demo notes  
4.7 UV‐Fluorescent Inks and Black Lights  
  • Use UV‐reactive markers or paints to draw simple symbols only visible under a UV lamp  
  • Compare to ordinary fluorescent paper under the same lamp  
4.8 Simulating Intaglio (Raised) Printing  
  • Create a rubber‐stamp plate from craft foam or carve linoleum, ink heavily and stamp onto thick paper  
  • Emphasize tactile raised lines  
4.9 Serial Number Patterns  
  • Generate pseudo‐serials in spreadsheet software, print in monospaced font  
  • Show how authorities check font consistency and sequence logic  
4.10 Combined Classroom Activity  
  • Divide students into “bank” and “inspector” teams  
  • “Bank” issues mock‐notes featuring selected simulated features; “inspectors” use magnifiers, UV lights, and touch tests to classify notes as “genuine” or “defective”

5. Ethical and Legal Considerations  
• Always mark demonstration notes clearly “Specimen” or “Educational Use Only.”  
• Avoid using real currency dimensions, colors, or design elements.  
• Emphasize the social harm of counterfeiting and the importance of legal compliance.  
• Collaborate with local law‐enforcement liaisons if planning public exhibitions.

6. Conclusion  
• Understanding detection methods and security features deepens financial literacy and public trust.  
• Safe, classroom‐scale simulations reinforce learning without facilitating illicit counterfeiting.  
• Ethical framing ensures respect for legal boundaries and the societal role of secure currency.
